book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life

chapters.file: ch16 - How We Still Might Manage a Smile Being Pirates and Making Meaning.md
chapters.relation: Adam Glover reads 'A Pirate Looks at Forty' through Kristeva's intertextuality: since every text and self is a 'mosaic of quotations' pirated from pre-existing sources, Buffett's confession that he was born 'two hundred years too late' makes him an ironic pirate who can no longer believe or plunder unselfconsciously, unlike the oblivious common-sense pirate. Invoking Barthes's death of the author, he argues the pirate's life is a hard freedom to improvise multiple meanings (the ever-changing 'head uptown' variations in the song) with full responsibility for one's choices. The chapter ends weighing Camus's worry that meaninglessness makes life not worth living against the Nietzsche of The Birth of Tragedy, who answers that the meaning of life is life itself, and it sides with Buffett against Socrates's 'unexamined life' while admitting it cannot settle the question.

chapters.file: ch17 - An Altar Boy’s Public Penance.md
chapters.relation: Flamm and Rea take Buffett's altar-boy grudge against Catholic moralism — the 'bakers' of 'Fruitcakes' who try to cure humanity's half-baked madness — and frame it with Nietzsche's charge that 'there was only one Christian, and he died on the cross.' They then cast Buffett as a latter-day Spinoza: like the excommunicated lens-grinder he rejects the orthodox God, finds God in nature ('One Particular Harbor' as a view 'sub specie aeternitatis'), and treats wealth, honor, and sensual pleasure ('Cheeseburger in Paradise') as means toward the greatest happiness rather than sins. Nietzsche's Dionysian intoxication ('God's Own Drunk') and Shakespeare's Sir Toby versus the moralist Malvolio support embracing natural madness, and the chapter closes by arguing Buffett's confessional songs ('Coastal Confessions') make his Parrothead audience the priest who grants the altar boy's public penance and forgiveness.

chapters.file: ch19 - “Happily Ever After, Now and Then”.md
chapters.relation: Erin McKenna explains how a feminist can love Buffett by reading 'Fins' and 'Why Don't We Get Drunk (and Screw)' as critiques of predatory land sharks rather than endorsements, and 'Margaritaville' as a man admitting 'it's my own damn fault.' Against Rousseau's pliable helpmate ideal of woman she sets Wollstonecraft's Vindication — equal education and personhood for women — and Charlotte Perkins Gilman's pragmatist-feminist case that women's economic, physical, and mental dependence stunts everyone. Buffett's novels then pass the Gilman test: Desdemona, Trevor Kane, Cleopatra Highbourne, and Sophie are smart, independent women, and the male leads must reform their habits to earn them, aiming at Desdemona's 'happily ever after, now and then' instead of the fairy-tale ending.

chapters.file: ch20 - The Fruitcake as Performative Exemplar.md
chapters.relation: John Kaag pairs Buffett's 'Fruitcakes' with Judith Butler's constructivism: institutions 'girl' infants through interpellation (the sonogram naming), the heterosexual imperative abjects gay, lesbian, and transgender 'nobodies,' and these excluded fruitcakes are the cosmic baker's half-baked people. The movie-theater stanza ('a twelve pound Nestle Crunch for twenty-five dollars') becomes Heidegger's das Man, others thinking and choosing for us, while Buffett's 'mea culpa' refrain and 'Religion's in the hands of some crazy-ass people' attack the guilt constitutive of Christian subjecthood, with Dewey's broad, doctrine-free religious experience offered as common ground. Buffett concerts themselves are read as performative exemplars — drag-show-like borderland communities where four generations act out the 'little bit of fruitcake' in everyone as a quiet political protest against enforced normalcy.

chapters.file: ch22 - Wonder Why We Ever Go Home.md
chapters.relation: Duke Richey maps Buffett's West — 'Ringling, Ringling,' the Rancho Deluxe soundtrack, Tully Mars — onto Josiah Royce's philosophy of community: only people who root in a place, face its history ('wise provincialism'), and sacrifice selfish desires for the whole can build Beloved Communities, a lesson enacted when cattle rustlers Jack and Cecil accept community sanction and find belonging working the Rancho Deluxe. Wallace Stegner's coral-reef metaphor from Angle of Repose supplies the image of communities built up millimeter by millimeter yet still vulnerable to pollution and over-fishing, with Royce's environmental regret (covering 'the wounds' of the landscape with gardens) anticipating the chapter's sustainability ethic. 'Wonder Why We Ever Go Home' thus asks what we really seek when we seek grace through community: not the nomadic Pickup Truck Death of every-man-for-himself, but cooperation that makes a society to match the scenery.

chapters.file: ch23 - “Where Did All the Good Songs Go ”.md
chapters.relation: Scott Pratt answers whether 'Margaritaville' is art by rejecting object-based theories (Kivy's score-compliance, the abstract perfect performance, the unrecorded instance that vanishes) for Dewey's Art as Experience: art is 'an experience,' complete and self-sufficient, followed by a reflective, evaluative second phase. He reads 'Makin' Music for the Money' as moving from solitary self-interested music-making to a community of musicians, and the Port of Spain steel-drum rehearsal of 'King of Somewhere Hot' that carried forward into the Miami concert as Dewey's two phases in action. Buffett's fly-fishing stories — the lost blue marlin that became 'a story,' the released Long Island bass that 'replenished his saline psyche' — supply Haeckel's ecological model in which music, like fishing, is an organism-environment interaction, making songs 'homemade' eco-music that belongs to listeners in its own ecosystem.

chapters.file: ch24 - “Livin’ and Dyin’ in Three-Quarter Time”.md
chapters.relation: Randall Auxier uses Buffett's catalog to think about fortune and fate, reading Buffett's bold career moves (walking out on Nashville for the beach, later annexing it via 'It's Five o'Clock Somewhere') through Machiavelli's advice to marry Fortuna and master her tricks with virtù. Against Aristotle's demanding answer that only aretē, moral excellence, defends happiness against bad luck, he takes Vico's middle path: natural causes, moral causes, and the occasions of fortune are gathered under providence, so Buffett's seaplane crash ('God, Buddha, St. Christopher, my guardian angel... luck, and the United States Navy water-survival training') shows any fate can be turned to good ends for others. Sorting Buffett's songs into places, times, meetings, sentiments, and thoughts — the key sentiment being the wistful — the chapter lands on contentment as gratitude: being 'livin' and dyin' in three-quarter time.'

chapters.file: ch25 - Songs Referred to in This Book.md

holes.name: Julia Kristeva
holes.what: Bulgarian-French theorist who founded intertextuality theory: every text is a 'mosaic of quotations' reweaving pre-existing texts, so no author controls meaning.
holes.why: Chapter 16 defines Buffett's piracy and his being 'two hundred years too late' entirely through her intertextuality theory.

holes.name: Intertextuality
holes.what: The doctrine that all writing, thinking, and selves are rearrangements of already-existing words and ideas rather than original creations.
holes.why: Chapter 16 needs it to turn Buffett's pirate into the ironic pirate whose self is stitched from borrowed cultural texts.

holes.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
holes.what: Pragmatist feminist (1860-1935) who argued that women's economic, physical, and mental dependence on men stunts the development of the whole species (Women and Economics, Herland).
holes.why: Chapter 19 uses her dependence and dress-reform critique as its main lens for judging the women in Buffett's songs and novels.

holes.name: Josiah Royce
holes.what: American absolute idealist (1855-1916) whose philosophy of community holds that individuals find salvation only in Beloved Communities bound by shared memories and hopes.
holes.why: Chapter 22 reads Buffett's western songs and Rancho Deluxe as Roycean lessons about community and 'wise provincialism.'

holes.name: The Philosophy of Community (Beloved Community)
holes.what: Royce's doctrine that humane societies arise only where individuals sacrifice selfish desires for the good of the whole.
holes.why: Chapter 22 applies it to 'Ringling, Ringling' and Rancho Deluxe to argue belonging, not rugged individualism, redeems Western boomtowns.

holes.name: Giambattista Vico
holes.what: Neapolitan philosopher (1668-1744) whose New Science steers between Stoic fate and Epicurean chance by explaining events through natural causes, moral causes, and providence.
holes.why: Chapter 24's resolution of Buffett's fortune-versus-fate puzzle rests on Vico's triad and his notion of providence.

holes.name: Providence
holes.what: Vico's idea that whatever is provided — the order of nature, formed character, and fortune's obstacles — can be turned to good ends, especially for others.
holes.why: Chapter 24 ends by defining contentment as gratitude for providence, the third term that reconciles Buffett's fate and fortune.
